meta.title: Who really said "Wherever you stand, be the soul of that place"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely credited to Rumi, but no Persian couplet or scholarly translation contains it. Wikiquote files it as attributed, citing only a 2009 self-help book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Wherever you stand, be the soul of that place'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Rumi everywhere, sourced nowhere. No Persian original, no named translator — Wikiquote's only citation is a 2009 self-help book.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The line is everywhere under Rumi’s name, and the thought is not out of character for him — but no Persian couplet and no scholarly English translation has been located that contains it. Wikiquote files it in its Attributed section, and the only printed source it can cite is Patricia Flasch’s Becoming a Love Dog: From Emptiness to Tenderness (2009), a self-help book inspired by Rumi rather than a translation of him. Nowhere that the line circulates does anyone name a work, a book of the Masnavi, a ghazal number, or a translator.

source.excerpt: Wherever you stand, be the soul of that place.
trail: We started where a specialist would already have settled it. Quote Investigator has no entry for this line, so the best existing research is Wikiquote — and Wikiquote does not put it in a sourced section. It sits under Attributed, with exactly one citation: Patricia Flasch, Becoming a Love Dog: From Emptiness to Tenderness (2009), p. 16. That is a 2009 book written in response to Rumi, not an edition or translation of him Wikiquote: Rumi ↗.

There is one more clue, and it argues against certainty rather than for it. In the Wikiquote page source, invisible to readers, an editor has left a hidden note beside the line floating Book 6 (Daftar-e Sheshom) of the Masnavi as a possible home — followed by a question mark. Nobody has closed that question, and no verse number has ever been supplied the page source ↗.

So we went to the Persian. Rumi’s verse is not lost or fragmentary — the Divan-e Shams alone runs to roughly forty thousand verses and is fully digitised and searchable on Ganjoor, alongside the complete Masnavi. Phrase searches of that corpus did not surface a couplet matching this line Ganjoor: Divan-e Shams ↗.

Then the aggregators, which is where the line actually lives. Goodreads carries it with the bare credit ‘— Rumi’ and warns on the same page that its quotations are added by users and not verified; Quotefancy names no publication, work or translator at all. A quote with millions of impressions and zero citations is the standard profile of an attribution invented downstream of the text Goodreads ↗.
source.cutTag: No located original — the line as it circulates
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to give, and that absence is the finding. A genuine Rumi line can be placed: a book and verse number in the Masnavi, or a ghazal number in the Divan-e Shams. This one arrives free-floating — no couplet before it, none after, no rhyme partner, no metre. It reads as a finished aphorism in English, which is not how Persian verse usually survives translation.
source.rightsNote: Rumi’s thirteenth-century Persian is long out of copyright, but that fact protects nothing here. For a translated author, rights attach to the specific English wording — and this English wording has no located translator, edition or date. Until someone can name the rendering it came from, its status simply cannot be determined, so we assert none: treat it as unsourced rather than as free-to-reuse public domain. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Rumi
author.heading: The most counterfeited poet in English
author.metaLine: 1207–1273 · Persian poet, Islamic scholar and Sufi mystic
author.bio: Jalal al-Din Muhammad Rumi was a thirteenth-century Persian poet, Islamic scholar and Sufi mystic, born in Wakhsh and settled for most of his life in Konya, in what is now Turkey. He left two vast bodies of verse — the six-book Masnavi and the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi, together tens of thousands of lines — plus the prose Fihi Ma Fihi, seven sermons and a collection of letters, all of which survive and are edited. That completeness is exactly why an unlocatable ‘Rumi quote’ counts against itself: there is a corpus to check, and it is checkable. He is nonetheless the most heavily counterfeited author on the English-speaking internet, largely because the best-known English Rumi consists of loose re-renderings made by writers who do not read Persian.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Nobody else claims this sentence, and no scholar has debunked it — but nobody can source it either. Rumi is the most heavily counterfeited author on the English-speaking internet, and this line carries every marker of the pattern except a smoking gun.

items.why: Wikiquote — which does maintain separate sourced sections for the Masnavi and the Divan-i Shams — puts this line in Attributed instead, backed by a single secondary citation to a 2009 self-help title see the section ↗.

Every high-traffic copy gives the name and nothing else — no book, no poem, no translator, no date. Goodreads itself flags that its quotations are user-submitted and not verified Quotefancy’s bare credit ↗.

items.who: A couplet with no manuscript behind it
items.why: At least one Persian-language teaching site now prints a Persian couplet for this line. It cites no book, manuscript or scholarly source for it, and the wording did not surface in searches of Ganjoor’s Rumi corpus. A Persian rendering produced from the English is not evidence of a Persian original the uncited couplet ↗.

The best-selling English Rumi is not translation. Coleman Barks calls his publications ‘versions’ or ‘re-renderings’ because he does not read Persian, working instead from earlier scholars’ English — in his own words, he has ‘nothing to be faithful to, except what the scholars give’. Once the chain back to the Persian is broken, sentences that were never Rumi’s can enter it and never be caught Ajam Media Collective ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: this may well be Rumi, and nothing rules it out — but nobody has yet produced the couplet. The test Rumi scholars actually apply is whether a verse appears in the earliest Persian manuscripts and in Foruzānfar’s critical edition; until this line is run through that test and found, ‘attributed’ is the most that can honestly be claimed Ibrahim Gamard on testing fake Rumi verses ↗.

context.heading: Why an unsourced Rumi line is a problem, not a mystery
lead: Rumi did not vanish into legend. He died in Konya in 1273 leaving two immense, continuously copied bodies of verse — the six-book Masnavi and the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi — along with the prose Fihi Ma Fihi, seven sermons and a body of letters. All of it survives, all of it is edited, and most of it is now searchable line by line. That completeness is unusual for a thirteenth-century poet, and it changes what silence means: when a sentence credited to a lost author cannot be found, that is just the state of the evidence; when a sentence credited to Rumi cannot be found, someone has to explain how it got out.

The reason so many cannot be found is structural. The Rumi most English readers have met arrived through writers who do not read Persian and who describe their own work as re-rendering rather than translation. Ibrahim Gamard, who does translate from the Persian, has spent years documenting popular ‘Rumi’ passages that turn out to be heavily altered or absent from the manuscripts altogether. In that ecosystem a warm, well-shaped English aphorism needs no Persian ancestor to acquire his name — it only needs to sound like him.
detailsBody: What would close it: a book-and-verse reference in the Masnavi, or a ghazal number in the Divan-e Shams, matched to a published English translation that renders the line this way. Anyone holding that reference would settle this page in a sentence.
What would not: another aggregator repeating the credit, a pin board, or a Persian couplet produced without a manuscript, edition or critical-text citation behind it.
context.pull: A genuine Rumi line comes with a book and a verse number. This one comes with a name and nothing else.
